Building on this network-level overview, the following section introduces several of the significant proteins identified in the enrichment analysis and considers their possible relevance to arthritis in a cautious, mechanism-based manner.

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.
ITGAV is among the most compelling arthritis-relevant proteins in this list because it sits at the interface of matrix remodeling, synovial cell adhesion, leukocyte trafficking, angiogenesis, and cytokine activation. These processes are central to inflammatory arthritis and joint destruction. In particular, the ability of alpha-V integrin complexes to mediate R-G-D-dependent activation of latent TGF-beta-1 is highly relevant, because TGF-beta signaling contributes to synovial fibroblast activation, tissue remodeling, osteophyte formation in some arthritides, and broader regulation of immune responses. Its broad ligand repertoire, including fibronectin, fibrinogen, osteopontin, laminin, and matrix metalloproteinase-2, further links ITGAV to the inflamed arthritic joint microenvironment, where extracellular matrix turnover and invasive pannus behavior are prominent. The additional roles of ITGAV:ITGB3 in growth factor and IL1B-related signaling strengthen the plausibility that this receptor can amplify inflammatory and reparative pathways in arthritis. Overall, ITGAV stands out as a strong candidate mediator of both structural damage and chronic synovial inflammation.[PubMed:10025398](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10025398) [PubMed:9827803](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9827803) [PubMed:25127859](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25127859) [PubMed:11323698](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11323698) [PubMed:24935931](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24935931) 

From matrix interaction and cytokine activation, the discussion naturally moves to a receptor directly embedded in one of the dominant inflammatory signaling axes in arthritis.

TNFRSF1B is highly relevant to arthritis because tumor necrosis factor signaling is a dominant pathogenic axis in inflammatory joint disease, especially rheumatoid arthritis. The receptor's capacity to regulate nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells and c-Jun N-terminal kinase places it directly within signaling pathways that drive synovial inflammation, cytokine production, leukocyte survival, and resistance to apoptosis in pathogenic stromal and immune cell populations. In arthritis, persistent activation of tumor necrosis factor-responsive pathways contributes to synovial hyperplasia, pain, cartilage degradation, and bone erosion. TNFRSF1B is particularly interesting because it is often associated with cell survival and immunoregulatory effects rather than purely cytotoxic signaling, suggesting that it may shape the chronicity of inflammation by sustaining activated immune cells or synovial fibroblasts. Its linkage to TNF receptor associated factor one and TNF receptor associated factor two and antiapoptotic ubiquitin ligases also supports a mechanistic connection to the abnormal persistence of inflammatory cells within arthritic tissue.

A related aspect of chronic joint pathology is localized proteolysis and tissue invasion, which makes the next candidate especially relevant.

PLAUR is notable in the context of arthritis because plasminogen activation and pericellular proteolysis are integral to extracellular matrix degradation, synovial invasion, and cell migration within inflamed joints. uPAR-driven localization of plasmin formation can facilitate breakdown of matrix barriers and promote activation of protease cascades that contribute to cartilage destruction and pannus invasion. Beyond proteolysis, PLAUR also mediates signal transduction, which may enhance inflammatory cell activation, fibroblast motility, and tissue remodeling. These features are particularly relevant to rheumatoid arthritis, where invasive synovial tissue erodes cartilage and bone. Thus, PLAUR potentially links inflammatory signaling with the degradative microenvironment that characterizes destructive arthritis.[PubMed:15677461](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15677461) 

In parallel with matrix degradation, sustained leukocyte entry into the synovium is another defining feature of inflammatory arthritis.

ADAM8 is of interest for arthritis because leukocyte extravasation into synovial tissue is a defining event in inflammatory joint disease. The accumulation of neutrophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes in the synovium and synovial fluid depends on coordinated adhesion, migration, and tissue entry, and proteins that facilitate this trafficking can materially influence disease severity. If ADAM8 promotes leukocyte extravasation, it may contribute to sustained synovitis by increasing immune cell recruitment into the joint. As a member of the ADAM family, it is also plausibly connected to proteolytic remodeling and cell-cell interaction pathways that are often dysregulated in arthritis. Although the provided annotation is brief, the trafficking-related function alone makes ADAM8 a biologically meaningful candidate in arthritis pathogenesis.

Beyond cell trafficking, innate immune sensing pathways may also help shape the inflammatory character of the joint environment.

CLEC4D stands out because it connects innate immune sensing to downstream inflammatory polarization pathways that are strongly implicated in arthritis. Its activation of spleen associated tyrosine kinase, caspase recruitment domain family member nine, and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells is particularly relevant, as these signaling modules are central to myeloid-cell-driven inflammation in arthritic synovium. Moreover, its ability to promote T helper type one and T helper type seventeen priming is important because T helper type seventeen-associated cytokine networks, especially those involving interleukin seventeen, are well-established contributors to synovial inflammation, osteoclast activation, and tissue damage. Even though CLEC4D is classically described in antimicrobial immunity, pattern-recognition receptors frequently participate in sterile inflammation through recognition of endogenous danger signals and amplification of myeloid activation. Therefore, CLEC4D may have meaningful relevance to inflammatory arthritis by enhancing antigen uptake, antigen presentation, and pathogenic cytokine programs in the joint.[PubMed:23602766](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23602766) [PubMed:23911656](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23911656) [PubMed:14971047](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14971047) 

Whereas the preceding proteins may promote inflammatory activation, the next molecule is notable because it may instead function as a counter-regulatory signal.

LAIR1 is important in arthritis because it represents an endogenous inhibitory checkpoint capable of restraining excessive immune activation. Arthritis pathogenesis often reflects an imbalance between activating and inhibitory immune signals, and LAIR1 has the potential to dampen multiple arms of the inflammatory response, including T-cell cytokine production, B-cell antibody output, and myeloid differentiation. Its suppression of interleukin two, interferon gamma, tumor necrosis factor, interleukin eight, and interleukin ten-related responses, together with inhibition of nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells signaling in myeloid cells, suggests that reduced LAIR1 activity could favor persistent synovitis, whereas intact or enhanced LAIR1 signaling might be protective. The induction of TGF-beta may be context-dependent in arthritis, potentially contributing either to immune regulation or to tissue remodeling or fibrosis, but the dominant theme is that LAIR1 functions as a brake on inflammation. For this reason, it is a particularly interesting molecule when considering mechanisms of immune tolerance failure in autoimmune arthritis.

This balance between inflammatory activation and inhibitory restraint is closely connected to the structural consequences of disease, particularly bone erosion.

OSCAR is one of the clearest arthritis-relevant proteins in the list because osteoclast differentiation is a central mechanism underlying bone erosion in rheumatoid arthritis and other erosive arthropathies. Proteins that promote osteoclastogenesis directly influence the balance between bone formation and bone resorption, and in inflammatory settings this balance shifts toward pathologic bone loss. Given its specific role in osteoclast differentiation, OSCAR likely contributes to the structural damage phase of arthritis rather than merely inflammation alone. This makes it especially important in diseases where radiographic progression and erosions are major clinical concerns. Even though no citation is provided in the input, the functional annotation itself strongly supports a mechanistic connection to arthritis-associated bone destruction.

In addition to osteoclast-related pathways, antibody-driven activation of myeloid cells may provide another route through which inflammation is amplified.

FCAR may be relevant to arthritis because Fc receptor-mediated immune activation is a key mechanism through which antibodies amplify inflammation. Although immunoglobulin A is less emphasized than immunoglobulin G in many arthritis models, immunoglobulin A-containing immune complexes can activate myeloid cells and promote cytokine release, potentially contributing to synovitis. This is especially pertinent in forms of arthritis where mucosal immunity and aberrant antibody responses are implicated. Because FCAR mediates cytokine production downstream of immunoglobulin binding, it could participate in the inflammatory amplification loop within joints or at extra-articular sites that influence disease initiation. Its importance is therefore moderate but biologically credible, especially in antibody-associated inflammatory arthritis.

The inflammatory landscape of arthritis is also influenced by systemic metabolic signals, which provides context for the next candidate.

RETN is potentially relevant to arthritis because it links systemic metabolic inflammation with innate immune cell recruitment. The chemotactic effect on myeloid cells is particularly important, as monocytes and macrophages are major drivers of synovial inflammation and cytokine production in arthritic joints. Resistin has also been broadly associated with inflammatory states, and its dual role in metabolism and immune activation fits well with the recognized intersection between metabolic dysfunction and chronic inflammatory disease. In arthritis, RETN could therefore contribute to both local leukocyte accumulation and the systemic inflammatory milieu that worsens disease activity. Its role may be especially pertinent in patients with obesity or metabolic comorbidity, where inflammatory adipokines can modify arthritis severity.[PubMed:15064728](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15064728) 

From this systemic perspective, it is also useful to consider proteins that may reflect the broader acute-phase response associated with chronic synovitis.

ORM1 is relevant to arthritis primarily as an acute-phase and immunomodulatory protein. Because inflammatory arthritis is characterized by systemic acute-phase responses, proteins such as ORM1 may reflect or influence disease activity. Its ability to modulate immune responses during the acute-phase reaction suggests that it could participate in the broader host response to chronic synovitis, even if it is not a direct driver of joint destruction. Thus, ORM1 is best viewed as a marker and possible modifier of inflammatory tone rather than a primary pathogenic effector. It may still be useful in interpreting arthritis-associated systemic inflammation.

Finally, returning to innate immune amplification, another lectin family receptor may be relevant through macrophage-centered inflammatory signaling.

Although the provided annotation focuses on dengue virus recognition, the most arthritis-relevant aspect of CLEC5A is its capacity to trigger macrophage inflammatory signaling and cytokine release through TYROBP-dependent pathways. Macrophage activation is a major determinant of synovial inflammation, and receptors that amplify cytokine production can have important pathogenic consequences even outside infectious contexts. Therefore, CLEC5A is of interest as a potential innate immune amplifier in arthritis, particularly if endogenous ligands or inflammatory microenvironments engage similar signaling outputs. Its relevance is more indirect than that of ITGAV, TNFRSF1B, or OSCAR, but it remains mechanistically plausible given the central role of macrophage-derived cytokines in joint disease.[PubMed:18496526](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18496526) [PubMed:21566123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21566123)

### Cytokines and inflammatory response (WP:WP530) 

The cytokine and inflammatory response pathway is a core immunobiological network that coordinates how tissues detect danger, recruit immune cells, amplify defense programs, and either resolve or perpetuate inflammation. Cytokines are soluble signaling proteins produced by immune cells and tissue-resident stromal cells, including macrophages, dendritic cells, T lymphocytes, fibroblast-like synoviocytes, and chondrocytes. Within this pathway, upstream inflammatory triggers activate intracellular signaling modules such as nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells, Janus kinase and signal transducer and activator of transcription, mitogen-activated protein kinase, phosphoinositide 3-kinase and protein kinase B, and related transcriptional regulators, leading to the production of interleukin one beta, interleukin six, tumor necrosis factor alpha, interleukin seventeen, interleukin twenty-three, interferons, chemokines, matrix-degrading enzymes, prostaglandins, and reactive oxygen species. These mediators shape leukocyte recruitment, endothelial activation, synovial hyperplasia, osteoclast differentiation, cartilage catabolism, and pain-related neuroimmune signaling. In healthy tissue, cytokine signaling is tightly controlled in both magnitude and duration; however, in arthritis this pathway becomes chronically dysregulated, creating a self-sustaining inflammatory niche within the joint. A notable feature of arthritic inflammation is that cytokines do not act in isolation but instead synergize across cell types. For example, tumor necrosis factor alpha cooperates with interleukin seventeen in synovial fibroblasts to induce chemokines and interleukin six, while interleukin one beta strongly drives catabolic and inflammatory responses in cartilage and synovium. Accordingly, this pathway appears to be central not only to disease pathogenesis across rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, osteoarthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and post-traumatic arthritis, but also to therapeutic intervention through biologic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs and small-molecule inhibitors.

Against this biological background, the provided literature collectively suggests that the cytokine and inflammatory response pathway is a central driver of arthritis initiation, amplification, tissue destruction, and therapeutic responsiveness. In rheumatoid arthritis, synovial fibroblasts emerge as active inflammatory effectors rather than passive structural cells: tumor necrosis factor alpha induces inflammatory programs, and the addition of interleukin seventeen A markedly amplifies production of interleukin six and neutrophil- and monocyte-recruiting chemokines through transcriptional regulators such as cut-like homeobox one and nuclear factor kappa B inhibitor zeta, demonstrating how cytokine synergy may sustain leukocyte influx and chronic synovitis (PubMed:32079724). Additional studies show that inflammatory stimuli in fibroblast-like synoviocytes activate nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells, p38, c-Jun N-terminal kinase, phosphoinositide 3-kinase and protein kinase B, and oxidative stress pathways, leading to increased release of interleukin one beta, interleukin six, tumor necrosis factor alpha, interleukin eight, monocyte chemoattractant protein one, and matrix metalloproteinases, thereby linking cytokine signaling directly to cartilage degradation and bone erosion (PubMed:35309353, PubMed:31010320, PubMed:32510258, PubMed:30897288). The pathway is also supported clinically by therapy, as biologic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs that neutralize tumor necrosis factor alpha, interleukin six, interleukin seventeen A, and interleukin twelve or interleukin twenty-three improve inflammatory arthritis, suggesting that these cytokines are not merely biomarkers but likely pathogenic mediators (PubMed:36430392). In post-traumatic arthritis, local interleukin one signaling appears especially important during the acute phase after joint injury, because intra-articular interleukin one receptor antagonist reduced cartilage degeneration and synovial inflammation, whereas tumor necrosis factor inhibition did not confer similar benefit, indicating a context-specific hierarchy within the cytokine network (PubMed:24964765). In osteoarthritis, interleukin one beta induces chondrocyte inflammatory and catabolic responses, including interleukin six, tumor necrosis factor alpha, nitric oxide, prostaglandin E two, matrix metalloproteinase thirteen, and a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with thrombospondin motifs five through nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation, supporting the view that even degenerative arthritis may contain a substantial cytokine-driven inflammatory component (PubMed:31293216). In psoriatic arthritis, elevated serum interleukin twenty-three reflects a myeloid inflammatory signature and predicts response to phosphodiesterase four inhibition, highlighting the relevance of the interleukin twenty-three to interleukin seventeen axis and the potential value of cytokine profiling for patient stratification (PubMed:39697337). Studies of synovial fluid and local antigen-presenting cells further indicate that the arthritic joint constitutes a specialized inflammatory microenvironment in which conventional dendritic cells type two and monocytes, rather than all dendritic cell subsets equally, produce strong pro-inflammatory cytokine programs and promote interleukin seventeen-associated T-cell responses (PubMed:36685500). Biomarker-oriented work also shows that pro-inflammatory cytokines induce soluble interleukin seven receptor production in rheumatoid arthritis fibroblast-like synoviocytes, and higher serum levels are associated with poor response to tumor necrosis factor blockade, emphasizing that cytokine pathway activity may influence treatment resistance as well as disease severity (PubMed:21129157). More broadly, review articles comparing coronavirus disease 2019 with rheumatoid arthritis underscore that many of the same cytokines, especially interleukin six, interleukin one beta, tumor necrosis factor, and Janus kinase-dependent signals, define pathogenic inflammation in arthritis and have become therapeutic targets because of their central position in this pathway (PubMed:32561873). Taken together, these publications indicate that arthritis is fundamentally shaped by dysregulated cytokine networks operating across immune cells, stromal cells, and joint-resident structural cells, with disease-specific variations in dominant mediators but a shared outcome of persistent synovial inflammation, immune cell recruitment, matrix destruction, and progressive joint damage.[PubMed:32561873](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32561873) [PubMed:32079724](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32079724) [PubMed:36430392](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36430392) [PubMed:24964765](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24964765) [PubMed:35309353](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35309353) [PubMed:31293216](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31293216) [PubMed:39697337](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39697337) [PubMed:39981237](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39981237) [PubMed:21129157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21129157) [PubMed:36685500](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36685500) [PubMed:31010320](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31010320) [PubMed:32510258](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32510258) [PubMed:30897288](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30897288) 

Consistent with the literature synthesis above, the enrichment analysis identified 7 arthritis-associated proteins significantly enriched in the cytokine and inflammatory response pathway, indicating a compact but biologically focused signal centered on immune communication, inflammatory amplification, and tissue-destructive processes within the joint. This pathway appears quantitatively important because it integrates upstream danger sensing with downstream production of interleukin one beta, interleukin six, tumor necrosis factor alpha, interleukin seventeen, interleukin twenty-three, interferons, chemokines, matrix-degrading enzymes, prostaglandins, and reactive oxygen species, all of which contribute to leukocyte recruitment, endothelial activation, synovial hyperplasia, osteoclast differentiation, cartilage catabolism, and pain-related neuroimmune signaling in arthritis. Given that the enrichment is supported by 7 proteins, the analysis suggests that this inflammatory signaling axis may capture a substantial proportion of the disease-relevant functional connectivity identified in the present protein set, consistent with the central role of chronic cytokine dysregulation across rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, osteoarthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and post-traumatic arthritis.

To complement this pathway-level interpretation, we also include the protein-protein interaction network visualization for these 7 proteins together with the corresponding STRING webpage link for direct inspection of network connectivity and evidence structure.

![PPI Network](imgs/6665d15f-c2bb-46a2-afbb-92dc1142fb76.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=9AF2A7E78C3B96D8)

Building on this network view, the function enrichment analysis identified several significant proteins, which are introduced in detail below. IL12B appears highly relevant to arthritis because its annotated functions converge on several core processes implicated in inflammatory joint disease, namely cytokine regulation, autophagy, innate immune activation, and oxidative stress control. Of particular importance is its reported non-autophagic role in mediating the shuttle of interleukin twelve to late endosomes for secretion (PubMed:34374750). Interleukin twelve is a central pro-inflammatory cytokine that promotes T helper one-type immune responses and can amplify chronic synovial inflammation, making regulation of its secretion potentially important in arthritis pathogenesis, especially in immune-mediated forms such as rheumatoid arthritis. In parallel, IL12B also participates in selective autophagy by recognizing ubiquitinated cargo and promoting delivery to autophagosomes, while influencing aggregate formation and intracellular protein quality control (PubMed:31916398, PubMed:34374750). This is notable because defective autophagy has been linked to persistence of inflammatory signaling, altered synoviocyte behavior, and tissue damage in arthritic joints. Its ability to modulate innate immunity through targeting ubiquitinated interferon regulatory factor three for autophagic degradation further suggests a mechanism by which IL12B may restrain excessive type one interferon responses, which are increasingly recognized as contributors to autoimmune inflammation. Moreover, under oxidative stress, IL12B promotes sequestosome one accumulation and activates the kelch-like ECH-associated protein one and nuclear factor erythroid two-related factor two antioxidant pathway (PubMed:31916398), a function that may be especially relevant in arthritis because oxidative stress is a major driver of synovial inflammation, chondrocyte dysfunction, and cartilage degradation. Taken together, IL12B is notable not because it maps to a single pathway, but because it sits at the intersection of inflammatory cytokine secretion, stress adaptation, and autophagic control, all of which are mechanistically relevant to arthritis development and progression.[PubMed:31916398](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31916398) [PubMed:34374750](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34374750)

### Arthritis (HP:0001369) 

Arthritis is the pathological state of joint inflammation and encompasses a spectrum of disorders in which immune activation, stromal remodeling, vascular changes, and tissue-destructive programs converge within synovial and periarticular structures. In inflammatory arthritis, especially rheumatoid arthritis, the synovial membrane becomes hyperplastic and infiltrated by diverse immune cell populations, including T lymphocytes, B lymphocytes, myeloid cells, and activated fibroblasts, which together generate a cytokine-rich microenvironment that sustains pain, swelling, stiffness, cartilage injury, and bone erosion. Recent single-cell analysis of rheumatoid arthritis synovium has shown that inflamed joints are not uniform but instead segregate into distinct cellular abundance phenotypes defined by different combinations of immune and stromal cell states, indicating that joint inflammation is biologically heterogeneous and dynamically regulated across patients. This inflammatory pathway is also clinically important because it links local joint pathology to systemic consequences, including disability, impaired quality of life, cardiovascular risk, osteoporosis, and premature mortality. Therapeutically, suppression of joint inflammation through early diagnosis, treat-to-target disease-modifying treatment, and selective inhibition of key inflammatory mediators such as tumor necrosis factor, interleukin 6, and Janus kinase signaling can prevent or markedly slow irreversible structural damage, although efficacy and safety differ among treatment classes and patient populations.  

Building on this general framework, the provided literature further supports the view that joint inflammation represents a central biological process through which immune dysregulation is translated into synovitis, pain, cartilage degradation, bone erosion, and long-term disability. In rheumatoid arthritis, inflamed synovium contains multiple pathogenic immune and stromal cell states, and large-scale single-cell profiling demonstrates that patients can be stratified into distinct inflammatory tissue phenotypes with different cytokine patterns, risk-gene associations, histological features, and treatment responses, suggesting that arthritis may be driven by heterogeneous but convergent inflammatory programs within the joint microenvironment. This concept is consistent with broader mechanistic reviews showing that rheumatoid arthritis progresses through stages of immune triggering, maturation, tissue targeting, and fulminant synovial disease, culminating in hyperplastic synovium, destructive pannus formation, cartilage damage, and osteoclast-mediated bone loss. The clinical importance of this pathway is further underscored by treatment evidence indicating that early and intensive suppression of inflammation can prevent progression of irreversible joint injury in a large proportion of patients, with methotrexate-based strategies and subsequent biologic or targeted synthetic disease-modifying therapies directed against tumor necrosis factor, interleukin 6, or Janus kinase pathways substantially improving remission rates. At the same time, therapeutic studies also indicate that modulation of inflammatory signaling must be balanced against systemic safety, as Janus kinase inhibition with tofacitinib was associated with higher rates of major adverse cardiovascular events and malignancy than tumor necrosis factor inhibition in a high-risk rheumatoid arthritis population. Beyond rheumatoid arthritis, the inflammatory joint pathway may also be relevant across arthritides, including osteoarthritis and obesity-associated arthritis, in which inflammatory and metabolic signals can amplify symptoms and structural progression; accordingly, glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists are being investigated for anti-inflammatory and chondroprotective effects. Population-level data further emphasize the significance of this pathway, as rheumatoid arthritis remains a major and growing global cause of years lived with disability, highlighting that persistent joint inflammation is not only a local tissue process but also a major public health burden. Collectively, these studies indicate that arthritis is fundamentally linked to a joint-centered inflammatory pathway that is cellularly heterogeneous, mechanistically destructive, clinically targetable, and systemically consequential.[PubMed:37938773](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37938773) [PubMed:29736302](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29736302) [PubMed:30285183](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30285183) [PubMed:23172750](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23172750) [PubMed:35081280](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35081280) [PubMed:41034339](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41034339) [PubMed:37795020](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37795020) [PubMed:25212687](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25212687) [PubMed:37222927](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37222927) 

Against this background, the enrichment results provide a focused molecular perspective on the same inflammatory and tissue-remodeling processes. There were 17 arthritis-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of joint inflammation, a disease process characterized by synovial hyperplasia, immune cell infiltration, cytokine amplification, stromal remodeling, cartilage destruction, and bone erosion. This enrichment supports the biological relevance of the analyzed protein set because arthritis pathology is driven by the coordinated action of immune and stromal compartments within synovial and periarticular tissues, and the identification of 17 proteins within this inflammatory context suggests a compact but potentially highly interconnected functional module linked to disease activity, tissue injury, and systemic complications. The pathway description further emphasizes that inflammatory arthritis is not a uniform condition but a heterogeneous state shaped by distinct cellular abundance phenotypes across patients, suggesting that these 17 proteins may capture key components of immune activation, fibroblast pathogenicity, vascular adaptation, and tissue-destructive signaling that together contribute to pain, swelling, stiffness, disability, cardiovascular risk, osteoporosis, and premature mortality. We will introduce these proteins in detail in the following.

To facilitate interpretation of these relationships, the figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network of the 17 enriched proteins, together with the corresponding STRING webpage link for interactive network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/ab505c72-900f-4733-a1d1-b166fc0adc0e.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=DB9AD8B6CFA2C75A)

With this network context in place, the following section describes several proteins that may be especially relevant to arthritis-related biology identified during the function enrichment analysis. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

TNFRSF11B stands out as the protein with the clearest and most direct relevance to arthritis because it is centrally linked to osteoclast biology and bone remodeling, processes that are fundamental to structural joint damage. The described function indicates a role in osteoclast differentiation and activation through prolonged Ca2+ signaling, NFATC1 nuclear translocation, and osteoclast-specific gene transcription, which are hallmark mechanisms of bone resorption. In inflammatory arthritides such as rheumatoid arthritis, excessive osteoclast activation drives periarticular bone erosion, making this pathway highly disease-relevant. Its additional role in dendritic cell–T-cell interactions further strengthens its relevance, since arthritis pathogenesis is strongly shaped by crosstalk between innate and adaptive immunity. Thus, this protein connects two major pathogenic axes of arthritis: immune activation and osteoclast-mediated skeletal destruction.[PubMed:22664871](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22664871) 

From this osteoclast-centered perspective, it is also important to consider proteins that may contribute more directly to inflammatory cell recruitment and matrix injury within the joint. PRTN3 is highly relevant to arthritis because it integrates neutrophil-driven inflammation with tissue-destructive proteolysis. Its ability to degrade multiple extracellular matrix proteins, including several collagens, suggests a plausible contribution to cartilage and periarticular matrix damage in inflamed joints. This is particularly important in forms of inflammatory arthritis in which neutrophils accumulate in synovial fluid and contribute to protease-rich microenvironments. The reported roles in neutrophil transendothelial migration and inflammatory signaling via ADGRG3 and F2RL1/PAR-2 further support a mechanistic connection to synovitis, where leukocyte recruitment and endothelial interactions are critical early events. Therefore, PRTN3 may contribute both to inflammatory amplification and to structural tissue injury in arthritis.[PubMed:2033050](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2033050) [PubMed:28240246](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28240246) [PubMed:3198760](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3198760) [PubMed:23202369](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23202369) [PubMed:22266279](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22266279) [PubMed:36302784](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36302784) 

In parallel with neutrophil-associated mechanisms, adaptive immune activation provides another major axis through which chronic synovial inflammation may be sustained. CD79B is notable in the context of arthritis because B-cell receptor signaling is a major driver of adaptive immune activation, autoantibody production, and chronic synovial inflammation, especially in rheumatoid arthritis. The described function emphasizes its role in transmitting antigen-dependent BCR signals, supporting NF-kappa-B activation and downstream kinase signaling. These pathways are directly relevant to autoimmune arthritis, where aberrant B-cell activation promotes pathogenic autoantibodies, antigen presentation, and cytokine production. The importance of B cells in arthritis is further underscored by the clinical efficacy of B-cell-targeted therapies. Accordingly, CD79B represents a plausible mechanistic link to arthritis through its contribution to B-cell activation and maintenance of autoimmune responses.[PubMed:12563261](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12563261) [PubMed:14662906](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14662906) [PubMed:2404338](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2404338) [PubMed:7608542](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7608542) [PubMed:7690139](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7690139) [PubMed:9636152](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9636152) [PubMed:7592958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7592958) [PubMed:9177269](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9177269) [PubMed:7565679](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7565679) 

Shifting from immune signaling to structural tissue integrity, cartilage-associated proteins may provide complementary insight into joint vulnerability and progression. COL9A1 is directly relevant to arthritis because it encodes a structural constituent of hyaline cartilage, the tissue primarily degraded in many joint diseases. Although the provided annotation is concise, its biological importance is substantial: cartilage integrity depends on specialized extracellular matrix components, and disruption of these components can compromise tensile properties, resilience, and joint function. In osteoarthritis, progressive cartilage degeneration is the central pathological feature, and proteins that contribute to cartilage architecture are therefore of high interest. COL9A1 may be particularly informative as a marker of cartilage vulnerability or matrix remodeling, even if the annotation does not explicitly describe inflammatory signaling.

A related but somewhat more indirect line of reasoning involves pathways that may modulate inflammation, vascular responses, or symptom expression without being core structural determinants. ADA2 is of potential interest to arthritis because adrenergic signaling can modulate immune responses, vascular tone, and nociceptive pathways, all of which influence joint inflammation and pain. Although the annotation does not directly mention arthritis, suppression of adenylate cyclase downstream of catecholamine signaling may affect leukocyte behavior, cytokine production, and synovial vascular responses. Neuroimmune interactions are increasingly recognized in inflammatory arthritis, and receptors that couple sympathetic signals to intracellular second messenger pathways may help shape disease activity or symptom expression. Its relevance is therefore more indirect than that of TNFRSF11B, PRTN3, or CD79B, but it remains biologically plausible in the broader context of arthritis pathophysiology.

Continuing with proteins linked more closely to matrix biology, enzymes involved in proteoglycan homeostasis may also be relevant to the structural dimension of arthritis. CANT1 is potentially relevant to arthritis because proteoglycan synthesis is essential for cartilage matrix composition and biomechanical function. Articular cartilage depends on proteoglycan-rich extracellular matrix to resist compressive loading, and impaired synthesis or accelerated loss of these molecules is a defining feature of degenerative joint disease. The described enzymatic role in nucleotide metabolism linked to proteoglycan synthesis suggests that CANT1 may influence cartilage homeostasis and matrix maintenance. While the annotation does not directly connect the protein to inflammation, altered proteoglycan production could contribute to cartilage fragility and susceptibility to degeneration, making CANT1 more relevant to structural aspects of arthritis, particularly osteoarthritis.

Beyond extracellular matrix and signaling pathways, regulatory proteins that shape transcriptional states may also have a subtler influence on chronic joint disease. LBR has a less direct but still potentially meaningful connection to arthritis through epigenetic regulation. The annotation emphasizes its role in recognizing repressive chromatin marks and contributing to chromatin organization and centromere-related functions. Epigenetic dysregulation is increasingly implicated in chronic inflammatory diseases, including arthritis, where altered transcriptional programs in synovial fibroblasts, macrophages, and lymphocytes sustain pathogenic inflammation and tissue invasion. Although no arthritis-specific mechanism is provided here, proteins that shape chromatin accessibility and gene repression may influence inflammatory cell identity and persistence within diseased joints. Thus, LBR is better viewed as a candidate modifier of disease-related gene regulation rather than a primary arthritis effector.[PubMed:19783980](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19783980) [PubMed:20231385](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20231385) 

Finally, it is also worth considering proteins whose relevance may emerge mainly in specific clinical contexts rather than across arthritis broadly. SCARB2 has a limited but potentially relevant connection to arthritis through infection-associated or post-infectious mechanisms. While the provided function is focused on viral entry, infectious triggers can precipitate or mimic inflammatory arthritis in susceptible individuals. Receptors involved in host–pathogen interactions may therefore be relevant in settings where viral infection contributes to immune activation, molecular mimicry, or transient arthritic symptoms. However, based on the current annotation, SCARB2 is not as compelling a candidate as proteins directly involved in osteoclastogenesis, B-cell signaling, neutrophil inflammation, or cartilage structure.

### extracellular matrix structural constituent (GO:0005201) 

The pathway termed extracellular matrix structural constituent refers to the molecular function of proteins and macromolecules that physically build, stabilize, and organize the extracellular matrix, thereby preserving tissue architecture, tensile strength, elasticity, hydration, and biomechanical resilience. In joint tissues, this function is especially important because articular cartilage, synovium, subchondral bone, tendons, and ligaments all depend on a highly specialized extracellular matrix for normal load bearing and movement. Major extracellular matrix structural constituents include fibrillar and network-forming collagens, aggrecan and other proteoglycans, glycosaminoglycan-rich molecules, and accessory matrix proteins such as biglycan and cartilage oligomeric matrix protein. These molecules do not merely provide passive support; they also regulate cell adhesion, mechanotransduction, growth factor sequestration, matrix assembly, and tissue repair. In healthy joints, a dynamic equilibrium exists between extracellular matrix synthesis, organization, and degradation. When this equilibrium is disturbed, the structural constituents of the matrix are fragmented, depleted, abnormally remodeled, or replaced by mechanically inferior material. Such changes alter tissue stiffness, lubrication, and cellular behavior, and can generate bioactive matrix fragments that further amplify inflammation and degeneration. Thus, the extracellular matrix structural constituent pathway is a central determinant of joint integrity and a key interface linking biomechanics, inflammation, remodeling, and repair.  

Against this biological background, the collected literature suggests that the extracellular matrix structural constituent pathway is fundamentally involved in arthritis because disease progression in both osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis is associated with disruption of the molecules that maintain joint matrix integrity. In osteoarthritis, cartilage destruction is characterized by progressive degradation of matrix constituents together with insufficient repair, and the resulting matrix fragments may themselves propagate inflammation, indicating that loss of structural extracellular matrix molecules is both a marker and a driver of disease evolution (PubMed:21119607). Studies of osteoarthritis also show that cartilage extracellular matrix anabolism is protective: interventions that restore the expression of sex determining region Y box 9, collagen type two alpha one chain, and aggrecan reduce cartilage damage, whereas inflammatory signaling suppresses matrix synthesis and promotes matrix-degrading enzymes such as a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with thrombospondin motifs five and matrix metalloproteinases (PubMed:32602381, PubMed:41633494, PubMed:30652828). In rheumatoid arthritis, the relationship appears to extend beyond cartilage to the synovial microenvironment. Synovial extracellular matrix is now recognized as a structural and regulatory framework whose altered composition and function may contribute directly to synovial hyperplasia, leukocyte recruitment, chronic inflammation, and tissue destruction (PubMed:37331300, PubMed:35076142, PubMed:20131230). Gene expression profiling of synovial fibroblasts demonstrated that several genes belonging to the extracellular matrix structural constituent category, including multiple collagens, biglycan, and tubulointerstitial nephritis antigen like one, are constitutively upregulated in rheumatoid arthritis compared with osteoarthritis, even after stimulation with tumor necrosis factor alpha or transforming growth factor beta one, supporting the concept of a stable disease-imprinted matrix-producing phenotype in rheumatoid arthritis synovial fibroblasts (PubMed:22682473). Complementing this, recent work describes rheumatoid arthritis as a self-reinforcing cycle of matrix sclerosis, excessive degradation, inflammatory amplification by matrix-derived danger signals, and renewed pathological remodeling, with extracellular matrix degradation products such as collagen fragments and cartilage oligomeric matrix protein emerging as candidate biomarkers of disease activity and structural progression (PubMed:41653212). Therapeutic studies further support a potentially causal relationship, because dihydroartemisinin alleviated rheumatoid arthritis while targeting the extracellular matrix structural constituent signaling context and reducing matrix metalloproteinase two and matrix metalloproteinase three in synovial tissue (PubMed:39257420). Across arthritis subtypes, therefore, this pathway appears to link the primary structural failure of cartilage and synovium to inflammatory signaling, aberrant fibroblast behavior, immune cell trafficking, and defective repair, making it a plausible mechanistic hub for pathogenesis, biomarker development, and matrix-directed therapy.[PubMed:21119607](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21119607) [PubMed:32602381](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32602381) [PubMed:41633494](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41633494) [PubMed:30652828](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30652828) [PubMed:37331300](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37331300) [PubMed:35076142](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35076142) [PubMed:20131230](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20131230) [PubMed:22682473](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22682473) [PubMed:41653212](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41653212) [PubMed:39257420](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39257420) 

Consistent with this literature context, there were 17 arthritis-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway termed extracellular matrix structural constituent. This represents a focused set of proteins linked to a core molecular function that is directly relevant to joint biology, because the extracellular matrix provides the structural framework required for cartilage integrity, synovial stability, subchondral bone support, and the biomechanical performance of tendons and ligaments. In arthritis, enrichment of 17 proteins in this pathway is biologically notable because extracellular matrix structural constituents govern tissue architecture, tensile strength, elasticity, hydration, and resistance to repetitive mechanical loading, all of which are progressively impaired during inflammatory and degenerative joint damage. The pathway description further indicates that these structural molecules include collagens, proteoglycans, glycosaminoglycan-rich components, and matrix-associated proteins that collectively regulate not only physical support but also cell adhesion, mechanosensitive signaling, growth factor retention, matrix assembly, and tissue repair, thereby placing this enriched protein set at the intersection of structural failure, inflammation, remodeling, and attempted regeneration in arthritis.

To further contextualize this enriched set, the figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 17 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct inspection of network connectivity and evidence-supported associations.

![PPI Network](imgs/b8236284-ef4d-4420-b54e-fb0a465938dc.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=5B922BEDB3069719)

Building on the enrichment and network overview, the function enrichment analysis identified several significant proteins that may warrant closer consideration. We introduce them in detail below.  
CHI3L1 is among the most compelling arthritis-relevant proteins in this list because its annotated functions converge on several core pathogenic mechanisms of inflammatory joint disease: tissue remodeling, chronic inflammation, macrophage polarization, and regulation of cell survival. Arthritis, particularly rheumatoid arthritis and some forms of osteoarthritis, is characterized by persistent synovial inflammation accompanied by extracellular matrix turnover and dysregulated repair responses. The reported role of CHI3L1 in tissue remodeling directly aligns with these processes. Its capacity to regulate T helper cell type two-associated inflammation, dendritic cell accumulation, and macrophage type two differentiation further suggests that it may shape the inflammatory milieu within arthritic joints, where myeloid and antigen-presenting cell populations critically influence disease persistence and resolution. In addition, its role in controlling apoptosis and stress responses is relevant because synovial hyperplasia and altered survival of stromal and immune cells are central features of arthritis pathology. Although the provided annotations emphasize mucosal and pulmonary contexts, the underlying biology—remodeling, inflammatory amplification, and host-response regulation—appears highly transferable to joint disease mechanisms, making CHI3L1 a strong candidate biomarker or mediator in arthritis-related tissue damage and repair.  

In a related extracellular matrix and stromal signaling context, TNC stands out as highly relevant to arthritis because it is an extracellular matrix glycoprotein with functions that map directly onto joint remodeling and inflammatory stromal activation. In arthritic tissues, matrix components are not merely structural; they actively regulate cell adhesion, migration, and inflammatory signaling. The ability of TNC to bind multiple integrins suggests that it can modulate interactions among synovial fibroblasts, immune cells, and endothelial cells within the inflamed joint microenvironment. Particularly important is its documented pro-angiogenic activity, as synovial angiogenesis is a hallmark of inflammatory arthritis and supports leukocyte recruitment, pannus formation, and persistence of chronic inflammation. Its broader role in tissue guidance and regeneration further supports its relevance to pathological remodeling processes in the joint. Thus, TNC is notable as a plausible contributor to both the structural and inflammatory dimensions of arthritis, especially through matrix-cell signaling and vascular expansion.[PubMed:19884327](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19884327)  

Continuing with structural matrix components, COL6A3 is potentially important in arthritis because collagen type six is a key extracellular matrix component that contributes to tissue architecture and cell-matrix interactions. In joint tissues, especially cartilage, synovium, and periarticular connective structures, matrix proteins influence mechanical integrity as well as cellular behavior. The annotation that collagen type six acts as a cell-binding protein suggests a role in anchoring cells to the surrounding matrix and regulating stromal cell responses. In arthritis, disruption of matrix composition and altered cell-matrix signaling contribute to cartilage degradation, synovial fibroblast activation, and aberrant repair. Although the functional annotation provided here is concise, the extracellular matrix localization and cell-binding property make COL6A3 a relevant structural and signaling candidate in arthritis pathogenesis, particularly in relation to tissue remodeling and altered biomechanical homeostasis.  

Along the same structural line, COL9A1 is directly relevant to arthritis because it is a structural constituent of hyaline cartilage, the specialized connective tissue that is progressively damaged in many arthritic disorders, especially osteoarthritis. Cartilage integrity depends on a highly organized extracellular matrix, and collagen type nine contributes to the stability and function of this network. Any perturbation in cartilage structural proteins can influence susceptibility to degeneration, matrix breakdown, and impaired load-bearing capacity. Therefore, among the proteins listed, COL9A1 is one of the clearest links to the anatomical substrate of joint disease. Its importance lies less in inflammatory signaling and more in structural vulnerability: proteins essential for cartilage composition are highly pertinent to arthritis because cartilage erosion is a defining pathological outcome.  

Moving from structural collagens to matrix-associated signaling regulators, EFEMP1 is particularly noteworthy for arthritis because its annotated activities connect growth factor signaling, cell migration, and chondrocyte biology. Epidermal growth factor receptor signaling has recognized effects on synovial stromal activation, tissue remodeling, and cartilage homeostasis. The ability of EFEMP1 to induce epidermal growth factor receptor autophosphorylation implies that it may amplify signaling pathways involved in proliferation, survival, and inflammatory remodeling within joint tissues. Even more directly relevant is the note that EFEMP1 may act as a negative regulator of chondrocyte differentiation. Since chondrocytes are the resident cells responsible for maintaining cartilage matrix, factors that impair their differentiation or homeostatic function may contribute to cartilage degeneration and failed repair in arthritis. Its additional roles in adhesion and migration further suggest possible involvement in synovial tissue remodeling and stromal cell behavior. Collectively, EFEMP1 may be important at the interface of cartilage pathology and aberrant tissue signaling in arthritic disease.  

A related signaling and tissue-remodeling candidate is IGFBP7, which is relevant to arthritis because it combines growth factor modulation, vascular biology, and cell adhesion—three processes central to joint inflammation and remodeling. The insulin-like growth factor axis contributes to cartilage metabolism, tissue repair, and synovial responses, so proteins that modulate insulin-like growth factor bioavailability may influence anabolic or catabolic balance in the joint. Its ability to stimulate prostacyclin production may also be significant, given the role of lipid mediators in inflammation and vascular tone. Most notably, IGFBP7 acts as a ligand for cluster of differentiation ninety-three in angiogenesis, a process strongly implicated in rheumatoid arthritis, where neovascularization sustains synovitis and leukocyte trafficking. Thus, IGFBP7 may contribute to arthritis through both stromal-vascular remodeling and altered growth factor signaling, making it a plausible mediator of chronic joint pathology.[PubMed:38218180](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38218180)  

From a connective tissue organization perspective, LTBP2 is of interest in arthritis primarily because of its possible role in connective tissue structure and matrix organization. Although the annotation does not explicitly mention inflammatory signaling, proteins involved in elastic-fiber architecture can influence the biomechanical properties of periarticular tissues, including ligaments, synovium, and other connective structures that support joint function. Arthritis is not solely a disease of cartilage; it also involves broad alterations in extracellular matrix composition and tissue mechanics. Therefore, LTBP2 may be relevant as a marker or contributor to structural remodeling within the arthritic joint environment. Its significance is likely greater in the context of chronic tissue remodeling and altered mechanical resilience than in direct immune activation.  

In a related growth factor regulatory framework, PRG2 is noteworthy in arthritis because it may regulate local insulin-like growth factor availability through proteolytic cleavage of insulin-like growth factor-binding proteins. The insulin-like growth factor system is important for cartilage maintenance, matrix synthesis, and tissue repair, and dysregulation of this pathway can influence whether joint tissues undergo regeneration or degeneration. By releasing bound insulin-like growth factor from insulin-like growth factor-binding protein four and insulin-like growth factor-binding protein five, PRG2 may alter the balance of anabolic signaling within cartilage or synovial tissues. This is potentially relevant to both osteoarthritis, where defective repair and matrix loss predominate, and inflammatory arthritis, where tissue destruction coexists with attempted remodeling. Thus, PRG2 may be mechanistically linked to arthritis through protease-mediated control of growth factor bioavailability in the joint microenvironment.  

Shifting to regulation of matrix degradation, TFPI2 is relevant to arthritis because matrix remodeling is a fundamental process in joint destruction and repair. Plasmin-dependent proteolytic cascades contribute to extracellular matrix degradation, activation of other proteases, and tissue invasion by activated synovial cells. By inhibiting plasmin and related proteolytic activities, TFPI2 may function as a brake on destructive remodeling in arthritic tissues. This is especially important in rheumatoid arthritis, where invasive synovial pannus erodes cartilage and bone, and in osteoarthritis, where protease-driven matrix turnover progressively compromises joint integrity. The connection to factor sevena and tissue factor also raises the possibility of interplay between coagulation-related pathways and inflammation, which are increasingly recognized in chronic joint disease. Therefore, TFPI2 stands out as a potentially protective regulator of pathological matrix degradation in arthritis.  

Extending this discussion to additional extracellular and vascular-associated proteins, SPON1 has a less direct but still potentially meaningful connection to arthritis through its functions in cell adhesion and vascular-associated biology. Cell adhesion molecules are central to tissue organization, stromal activation, and cell migration within inflamed joints. The annotation indicating relevance to vascular smooth muscle cells suggests a possible role in vascular remodeling, which may be pertinent because angiogenesis and vascular structural changes support chronic synovitis. Although SPON1 is better characterized in neural contexts in the provided description, its adhesive properties and association with vascular cells make it a plausible participant in the altered extracellular environment of arthritic tissues. Its arthritis relevance is therefore more inferential than that of cartilage- or inflammation-centered proteins, but it may still contribute to stromal and vascular remodeling.  

By contrast, CRELD1 appears to have only a limited and indirect connection to arthritis based on the provided annotation. Its documented role in acetylcholine receptor localization is primarily relevant to neuromuscular biology rather than joint inflammation or cartilage degeneration. However, because cholinergic signaling can influence immune regulation, one could speculate about a secondary relationship to inflammatory processes. Nevertheless, compared with extracellular matrix proteins, angiogenic mediators, and regulators of growth factor signaling in this list, CRELD1 does not stand out as a major arthritis-linked candidate from the available functional information.[PubMed:30407909](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30407909)  

Similarly, CD4 is immunologically important, but the functional annotations provided here are centered on viral receptor activity rather than its broader role in T-cell biology. In principle, cluster of differentiation four-positive T cells are highly relevant to autoimmune arthritis because adaptive immune activation is a major driver of synovial inflammation, particularly in rheumatoid arthritis. However, because the supplied evidence specifically concerns microbial infection and viral interactions, the direct arthritis connection cannot be strongly inferred from this annotation alone. Thus, despite its general immunological importance, CD4 is not among the strongest arthritis-specific proteins in the present list based on the provided functional descriptions.[PubMed:12089508](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12089508) [PubMed:16331979](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16331979) [PubMed:2214026](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2214026) [PubMed:9641677](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9641677) [PubMed:17346169](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17346169) [PubMed:7909607](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7909607)

### Signaling by Interleukins (REAC:R-HSA-449147) 

Signaling by interleukins is a core immunoregulatory pathway that coordinates communication among leukocytes, stromal cells, synovial fibroblasts, macrophages, osteoclast precursors, chondrocytes, and endothelial cells. Interleukins are secreted cytokines that bind specific cell-surface receptors and activate intracellular signaling networks, most prominently Janus kinase and signal transducer and activator of transcription signaling, nuclear factor kappa B signaling, mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, phosphoinositide three-kinase and protein kinase B signaling, inflammasome-associated pathways, and transcriptional feedback regulators such as suppressor of cytokine signaling proteins. Through these mechanisms, interleukin signaling controls inflammatory gene expression, leukocyte recruitment, helper T cell polarization, macrophage activation, synovial fibroblast proliferation and invasiveness, matrix metalloproteinase production, angiogenesis, osteoclast differentiation, cartilage catabolism, and bone remodeling. In arthritis, this pathway is not a single linear cascade but a densely interconnected cytokine network in which different interleukins can amplify, restrain, or redirect inflammation depending on cellular context. Pro-inflammatory interleukins such as interleukin one beta, interleukin six, interleukin seventeen, interleukin eighteen, and interleukin twenty-three generally sustain synovitis and structural damage, whereas receptor antagonists or regulatory interleukins can counterbalance these effects. The pathway therefore represents both a mechanistic framework for disease pathogenesis and a major therapeutic axis in inflammatory and degenerative joint disease.  

Building on this general framework, the collected publications further suggest that signaling by interleukins is centrally involved in arthritis, especially rheumatoid arthritis, by linking immune activation to persistent synovial inflammation, pannus formation, cartilage destruction, and bone erosion. Human genetic evidence supports a causal contribution of interleukin one beta and interleukin six to rheumatoid arthritis risk, while higher levels of interleukin six receptor antagonist and interleukin one receptor antagonist appear protective, strongly implicating this signaling system in disease initiation and persistence (PubMed:35066242). At the tissue level, interleukin-driven signaling activates rheumatoid arthritis fibroblast-like synoviocytes, which then produce interleukin six, matrix metalloproteinase three, matrix metalloproteinase nine, and other inflammatory mediators through nuclear factor kappa B and related pathways, thereby promoting invasive synovitis and matrix degradation; this is illustrated by studies showing that methyltransferase like three enhances fibroblast-like synoviocyte activation through nuclear factor kappa B, and that restoration of inhibitory regulators such as micro ribonucleic acid four hundred ten dash three prime suppresses tumor necrosis factor alpha, interleukin one beta, interleukin six, and matrix metalloproteinase nine release (PubMed:34295905, PubMed:30242542). Several studies further show that interleukin signaling converges on Janus kinase and signal transducer and activator of transcription modules in synovial and immune cells, where inhibition of Janus kinase one, Janus kinase two, Janus kinase three, signal transducer and activator of transcription one, signal transducer and activator of transcription three, or signal transducer and activator of transcription six reduces inflammatory cytokine production, synovial hyperplasia, and bone damage in collagen-induced arthritis models, supporting the pathogenic importance of this downstream arm of interleukin signaling (PubMed:35571141, PubMed:34758437, PubMed:34600581, PubMed:38199156, PubMed:31872186). The pathway also shapes adaptive immunity: interleukin twenty-seven has context-dependent effects, suppressing ectopic-like structure formation, helper T cell type seventeen differentiation, helper T cell type two differentiation, and osteoclastogenesis, yet potentially worsening synovitis by promoting helper T cell type one responses, illustrating that different interleukins can exert both protective and pathogenic actions within rheumatoid arthritis (PubMed:35058928). Likewise, interleukin eighteen receptor signaling promotes inflammatory cell infiltration, systemic cytokine production, and joint erosion, whereas genetic deletion of interleukin eighteen receptor alpha ameliorates experimental arthritis together with increased suppressor of cytokine signaling three expression, indicating that unchecked interleukin signaling sustains disease whereas endogenous feedback inhibition is protective (PubMed:31861496). Beyond rheumatoid arthritis, interleukin signaling is also relevant to other arthritides: interleukin twenty-three signaling is a recognized pathogenic axis in psoriatic arthritis, and interleukin nineteen appears to limit osteoarthritis progression by reducing inflammation and apoptosis in chondrocytes, indicating that the biological consequences of interleukin signaling vary across disease contexts and cell types (PubMed:30196070, PubMed:41103413). Overall, the literature supports the conclusion that signaling by interleukins is a master pathway in arthritis because it integrates innate and adaptive immune responses with stromal cell activation, angiogenesis, osteoclast differentiation, and tissue destruction, while also providing multiple validated and emerging therapeutic targets.[PubMed:35066242](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35066242) [PubMed:34295905](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34295905) [PubMed:35571141](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35571141) [PubMed:27919189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27919189) [PubMed:31872186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31872186) [PubMed:30196070](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30196070) [PubMed:34758437](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34758437) [PubMed:34600581](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34600581) [PubMed:31861496](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31861496) [PubMed:38199156](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38199156) [PubMed:30242542](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30242542) [PubMed:35058928](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35058928) [PubMed:41103413](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41103413) 

To connect this literature-based interpretation with the enrichment results, the pathway-level protein set provides a quantitative view of how broadly interleukin-associated biology may be represented in arthritis. There were 63 arthritis-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of signaling by interleukins, a central immunoregulatory network that quantitatively links leukocyte activation, stromal cell responses, synovial fibroblast expansion, macrophage polarization, osteoclast precursor differentiation, chondrocyte catabolism, endothelial activation, and tissue remodeling across inflamed joints. This enrichment involving 63 proteins supports a broad and densely connected disease module rather than an isolated signaling event, consistent with the major contribution of interleukin-driven inflammatory signaling to synovitis, cartilage degradation, angiogenesis, bone erosion, and chronic immune dysregulation in arthritis. The protein set size of 63 indicates substantial functional convergence on cytokine-mediated communication, with the pathway mechanistically spanning Janus kinase and signal transducer and activator of transcription signaling, nuclear factor kappa B signaling, mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, phosphoinositide three-kinase and protein kinase B signaling, inflammasome-related signaling, and suppressor of cytokine signaling-dependent feedback control, thereby capturing both inflammatory amplification and regulatory restraint within the arthritic microenvironment.

To further illustrate the connectivity within this enriched set of 63 proteins, the interaction network is shown below. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network of these 63 enriched proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here: [Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=2399D86CE14984FA).

![PPI Network](imgs/964d7e78-3dc3-42c9-85c4-ebe2435c661e.png)

With this network context in mind, the following section introduces several significant proteins identified during the function enrichment analysis and considers, in a cautious manner, how each may relate to arthritis biology. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

CD14 is one of the most arthritis-relevant proteins in this list because it sits at the interface between innate immune sensing and inflammatory cytokine production. In inflammatory arthritis, especially rheumatoid arthritis and some forms of infection-triggered or microbiome-associated joint inflammation, activation of TLR pathways in synovial macrophages and monocytes is a major driver of tumor necrosis factor, interleukin one, and interleukin six production. The documented role of CD14 in delivering lipopolysaccharide to the toll-like receptor four signaling complex and promoting myeloid differentiation primary response eighty-eight-dependent nuclear factor kappa B activation strongly supports its relevance to synovitis and chronic joint inflammation. Its additional capacity to cooperate with toll-like receptor two complexes broadens its importance to endogenous and microbial ligands that may accumulate in damaged joints. Taken together, CD14 may plausibly act as an amplifier of macrophage activation, cytokine release, and perpetuation of inflammatory cascades central to arthritis pathogenesis.[PubMed:16148141](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16148141) [PubMed:15895089](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15895089) [PubMed:8612135](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8612135) [PubMed:19362712](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19362712) 

Extending this theme of innate immune sensing, CLEC4D appears relevant to arthritis because it links pathogen recognition to downstream inflammatory and adaptive immune polarization. The spleen associated tyrosine kinase-caspase recruitment domain family member nine-nuclear factor kappa B axis and helper T cell type one and helper T cell type seventeen skewing described for CLEC4D are particularly notable, since helper T cell type seventeen-related immunity and myeloid activation are strongly implicated in inflammatory joint disease. Its function in antigen uptake and presentation further suggests a role in sustaining local immune activation within synovial tissue. Even when arthritis is not directly infectious, receptors such as CLEC4D may contribute to sterile inflammation by responding to danger-associated ligands or by shaping the inflammatory tone of infiltrating myeloid cells. Therefore, CLEC4D may represent a mechanistic bridge between innate sensing, antigen presentation, and pathogenic T-cell responses relevant to arthritis.[PubMed:23602766](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23602766) [PubMed:23911656](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23911656) [PubMed:14971047](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14971047) 

In a related manner, although the cited annotation emphasizes microbial infection, CLEC5A remains potentially relevant to arthritis because its core biological output is strong macrophage-driven inflammatory cytokine production via an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif-coupled pathway. Macrophage activation is a central feature of synovitis, and receptors that signal through TYRO protein tyrosine kinase binding protein can intensify local inflammatory circuits, osteoclastogenic signaling, and tissue damage. This may be especially important in arthritis settings where innate immune activation, viral triggers, or sterile activation of myeloid cells contributes to disease flares. CLEC5A therefore stands out less for joint specificity and more for its capacity to amplify inflammatory cytokine programs that are highly pertinent to arthritis pathophysiology.[PubMed:18496526](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18496526) [PubMed:21566123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21566123) 

Continuing with related myeloid receptors, CLEC6A is notable in the context of arthritis because it integrates several processes that are highly relevant to inflamed joints: innate immune receptor signaling, neutrophil activation, and inflammatory cell crosstalk. The ability of CLEC6A-associated complexes to induce spleen associated tyrosine kinase-caspase recruitment domain family member nine-nuclear factor kappa B signaling is important because these pathways drive cytokine production and pathogenic myeloid responses in arthritis. Its functional link to neutrophil activation is also significant, given the contribution of neutrophils to synovial fluid inflammation, protease release, and oxidative damage. In addition, platelet-immune interactions are increasingly recognized as contributors to synovitis. Collectively, CLEC6A may be viewed as a signaling hub that could support both acute inflammatory recruitment and chronic immune activation in arthritis.[PubMed:14764707](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14764707) [PubMed:19098920](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19098920) [PubMed:23602766](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23602766) [PubMed:17086186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17086186) [PubMed:9171347](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9171347) 

In contrast to these activating receptors, LAIR1 is particularly interesting for arthritis because it represents an endogenous brake on immune activation. The annotation indicates broad anti-inflammatory effects, including suppression of interleukin two, interferon gamma, interleukin eight, interleukin ten, tumor necrosis factor, immunoglobulin production, and nuclear factor kappa B signaling. In chronic inflammatory arthritis, failure of inhibitory checkpoints can permit persistent activation of synovial lymphocytes, myeloid cells, and dendritic cells. LAIR1 therefore stands out as a candidate counter-regulator whose reduced activity or ineffective signaling could contribute to loss of immune tolerance and sustained synovitis. Conversely, preservation or therapeutic enhancement of LAIR1-like pathways could potentially be beneficial by dampening cytokine production and antigen-presenting cell differentiation in the arthritic joint.

Shifting from cytokine and receptor control to lipid mediator biology, LTA4H is highly relevant to arthritis because it occupies a pivotal position in balancing inflammatory and pro-resolving pathways. Its generation of leukotriene B4 is especially important, as leukotriene B4 is a potent chemoattractant and activator of neutrophils, cells that are abundant in inflamed synovial fluid and contribute to joint swelling, pain, and tissue injury. At the same time, the annotation highlights a potentially protective side through degradation of the neutrophil attractant proline-glycine-proline and participation in resolvin biosynthesis. This duality is mechanistically important in arthritis, where disease severity often reflects an imbalance between inflammatory amplification and resolution. LTA4H therefore stands out as a regulator of leukocyte recruitment and inflammatory persistence in the joint.[PubMed:1881903](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1881903) [PubMed:9287304](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9287304) [PubMed:20813919](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20813919) 

A related but distinct aspect of arthritis biology involves cell adhesion and matrix interaction, which makes ITGAV strongly connected to disease mechanisms. Integrin-mediated adhesion, migration, and matrix interaction are central to synovial invasion and pannus formation. The annotation also highlights a particularly important feature: alpha-V-containing integrins activate latent transforming growth factor beta one, a cytokine with complex but major roles in tissue remodeling, fibrosis, osteoclast-osteoblast balance, and immune regulation in arthritic joints. In addition, alpha-V integrins support angiogenesis and wound-healing-like responses, both of which are hallmarks of hyperplastic rheumatoid synovium. Because these receptors bind multiple matrix proteins and growth factors, ITGAV likely contributes to the abnormal communication between synovial fibroblasts, endothelial cells, immune cells, and extracellular matrix that drives chronic joint destruction.[PubMed:10025398](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10025398) [PubMed:9827803](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9827803) [PubMed:25127859](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25127859) [PubMed:11323698](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11323698) [PubMed:24935931](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24935931) 

Consistent with this emphasis on tissue remodeling, the next entry appears to describe a vascular endothelial growth factor receptor pathway that may also be highly relevant to arthritis. Despite the apparent naming inconsistency in the provided annotation, the listed function clearly describes a vascular endothelial growth factor receptor pathway. Pathologic angiogenesis and increased vascular permeability are defining features of inflamed synovium, enabling persistent leukocyte influx and expansion of pannus tissue. The described signaling outputs, including endothelial migration, survival, actin remodeling, and induction of nitric oxide production, are all processes implicated in synovial hypervascularity and inflammatory edema. Vascular endothelial growth factor-driven signaling is well established as a contributor to rheumatoid arthritis progression, and proteins mediating these effects can influence both inflammation and structural joint damage. Accordingly, this entry stands out because vascular remodeling is a major component of arthritis pathogenesis.

This focus on structural damage leads naturally to OSCAR, which is one of the most directly arthritis-relevant proteins in the list because osteoclast differentiation is a central mechanism of bone erosion in inflammatory arthritis, especially rheumatoid arthritis. Bone destruction in arthritis is not merely a byproduct of inflammation; it is actively driven by osteoclastogenic pathways at the synovial-bone interface. A receptor that specifically regulates osteoclastogenesis therefore has immediate mechanistic relevance to structural damage, radiographic progression, and irreversible disability. OSCAR stands out because it links immune activation to skeletal pathology, making it particularly important for understanding erosive disease phenotypes.

Another protein that may connect inflammatory signaling with joint damage is PLA2G2A, which is highly pertinent to arthritis because it can directly fuel inflammatory lipid mediator production and influence cell-matrix signaling.
