By releasing arachidonic acid from phospholipids, PLA2G2A provides substrate for downstream synthesis of prostaglandins and leukotrienes, both of which are major mediators of pain, swelling, leukocyte recruitment, and tissue injury in arthritic joints. Its additional integrin-activating function suggests that it may also modulate synovial cell adhesion, migration, and proliferation, potentially contributing to pannus formation. The combination of enzymatic pro-inflammatory activity and non-catalytic signaling effects makes PLA2G2A a particularly compelling candidate in arthritis biology.[PubMed:10358193](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10358193) [PubMed:11694541](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11694541) [PubMed:8425615](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8425615) [PubMed:27292189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27292189) 

In a similar vein, PLAUR is relevant to arthritis because the urokinase plasminogen activator receptor system is closely linked to extracellular matrix remodeling, cell migration, and invasive behavior of synovial cells. In inflammatory arthritis, excessive pericellular proteolysis contributes to cartilage degradation, basement membrane disruption, and leukocyte trafficking into the joint. Beyond proteolysis, the signaling functions of PLAUR may support motility and activation of fibroblast-like synoviocytes and immune cells, thereby promoting chronic synovitis and tissue invasion. This makes PLAUR an important candidate for connecting inflammatory activation with structural joint damage.[PubMed:15677461](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15677461) 

Beyond matrix remodeling, humoral effector systems may also contribute to joint injury, and C9 stands out because complement activation is an established contributor to inflammatory arthritis. Formation of the membrane attack complex can promote direct tissue injury, amplify synovial inflammation, and enhance recruitment and activation of leukocytes. In arthritic joints, complement components can be activated by immune complexes and damaged tissue, thereby sustaining inflammatory cascades. As the pore-forming component of the terminal complement pathway, C9 is especially relevant to the effector phase of complement-mediated damage within synovium and cartilage.[PubMed:26841934](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26841934) [PubMed:9212048](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9212048) [PubMed:9634479](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9634479) [PubMed:30111885](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30111885) [PubMed:4055801](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/4055801) 

Balancing this pro-inflammatory complement activity, C4BPB is noteworthy in arthritis because it represents a counter-regulatory component of the complement system. Since excessive classical pathway activation can contribute to immune complex-driven synovitis and tissue damage, proteins that restrain complement activation may influence disease severity and the extent of bystander injury. The function of C4BPB suggests a protective role by limiting propagation of complement cascades in inflamed tissue. In arthritis, such regulators are important because disease outcome often depends not only on inflammatory triggers but also on the adequacy of endogenous mechanisms that contain tissue-damaging effector responses.

Resolution of inflammation is also shaped by cellular interactions, and ICAM3 is relevant to arthritis because leukocyte adhesion and clearance of apoptotic cells are both key determinants of whether inflammation resolves or persists. The ability of ICAM3 to mediate interactions with beta-2 integrins suggests a role in immune cell trafficking and cell-cell communication in synovial tissue. Particularly important is its contribution to macrophage phagocytosis of apoptotic neutrophils, a process central to resolution of inflammation. Defects in apoptotic cell clearance can prolong synovitis and promote secondary necrosis, thereby increasing inflammatory mediator release. ICAM3 therefore stands out as a molecule potentially linked to both inflammatory cell retention and defective resolution in arthritis.[PubMed:1448173](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1448173) [PubMed:23775590](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23775590) 

A related connection between myeloid activation and skeletal damage is suggested by the next entry. Although the provided functional description appears to correspond to the triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells two-associated adaptor pathway rather than triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells two alone, the biology described is highly relevant to arthritis. Two aspects are especially important: first, the promotion of myeloid and neutrophil activation, which can intensify synovial inflammation; second, the requirement for osteoclast cytoskeletal organization and multinucleation, which directly links this pathway to bone erosion. In inflammatory arthritis, osteoclast formation at the pannus-bone interface is a major cause of irreversible structural damage. Thus, this entry stands out because it integrates immune activation with osteoclastogenesis, two core processes in arthritis pathogenesis.[PubMed:15471863](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15471863) [PubMed:9647200](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647200) [PubMed:15728241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728241) [PubMed:16715077](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16715077) [PubMed:21727189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21727189) [PubMed:18957693](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18957693) [PubMed:18685038](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18685038) [PubMed:25690660](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690660) [PubMed:21257958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21257958) [PubMed:18691974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18691974) [PubMed:12569157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12569157) [PubMed:14969392](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14969392) [PubMed:17086186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17086186) 

This interplay between inflammatory signaling and tissue persistence is also reflected in TNFRSF1B, which is highly relevant to arthritis because tumor necrosis factor signaling is one of the central pathogenic pathways in rheumatoid arthritis and related inflammatory arthritides. The annotation emphasizes nuclear factor kappa B and c-Jun N-terminal kinase activation, both of which drive expression of inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, adhesion molecules, and matrix-degrading enzymes in synovial tissue. Its role in balancing survival and apoptosis is also important, since resistance of synovial fibroblasts and inflammatory cells to apoptosis contributes to chronic synovial hyperplasia. TNFRSF1B therefore stands out as a plausible mediator of sustained tumor necrosis factor-dependent inflammation and tissue persistence in arthritic joints.

Moving to a more indirect candidate, ADA2 is less directly established than classical immune mediators, but it may still be relevant to arthritis through neuroimmune regulation. Adrenergic signaling can shape leukocyte activation, vascular tone, and pain-related inflammatory responses. Because synovial inflammation is influenced by autonomic and catecholaminergic inputs, receptors that suppress adenylate cyclase signaling may alter inflammatory cell behavior or local vascular responses. This makes ADA2 an interesting, though more indirect, candidate in the broader pathophysiology of arthritis.

At the level of cellular mechanics, BAIAP2 is potentially relevant to arthritis because cytoskeletal remodeling is essential for migration and invasive behavior of immune cells and fibroblast-like synoviocytes. In rheumatoid arthritis, pathogenic synoviocytes acquire enhanced motility and tissue-invasive properties that depend on actin reorganization. A protein that supports cell division control protein forty-two homolog- and ras-related C3 botulinum toxin substrate one-dependent membrane dynamics may therefore contribute to leukocyte trafficking, pannus invasion, and possibly cartilage destruction. Although not a canonical arthritis gene, BAIAP2 stands out as a plausible regulator of the cellular mechanics underlying joint inflammation and tissue invasion.

Finally, BRK1 is of interest in arthritis because actin-remodeling machinery influences immune cell migration, phagocytosis, and the invasive phenotype of synovial fibroblasts. Through its role in the WASP family verprolin-homologous protein-Arp2/3 pathway, BRK1 may affect lamellipodia formation and cell motility, processes highly relevant to leukocyte recruitment into joints and pannus expansion across cartilage surfaces. While the cited annotation is not arthritis-specific, the underlying cytoskeletal function is mechanistically compatible with disease processes that depend on aberrant cell movement and tissue invasion.[PubMed:27605705](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27605705)

### Matrix metalloproteinases (WP:WP129) 

Matrix metalloproteinases are a family of zinc-dependent endopeptidases that mediate controlled degradation and remodeling of extracellular matrix components, including collagens, proteoglycans, gelatin, and other structural molecules of cartilage, synovium, tendon, and bone. They are synthesized as inactive precursor proteins and require post-translational activation, after which their activity is tightly restrained by tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases. In healthy joints, this proteolytic system contributes to physiological matrix turnover, tissue repair, and remodeling. In inflammatory and degenerative joint disease, however, the balance between matrix metalloproteinases and their inhibitors becomes disturbed, leading to excessive extracellular matrix destruction and altered cellular signaling. Beyond direct matrix cleavage, matrix metalloproteinases can regulate cytokines, chemokines, receptors, angiogenesis, oxidative stress responses, and immune cell behavior, thereby linking structural damage to inflammation and immunity. Distinct family members have partially specialized roles in arthritis: interstitial collagenases and stromelysins participate in cartilage collagen and proteoglycan degradation, gelatinases contribute to matrix remodeling and inflammatory cell migration, and collagenase thirteen is especially important in osteoarthritis because of its potent cleavage of type two collagen. Overall, current evidence places matrix metalloproteinases at the intersection of synovial inflammation, fibroblast pathogenic activation, cartilage erosion, bone destruction, and biomarker development, while also indicating that their net effect depends on disease context, timing, tissue localization, and the counterbalancing action of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases.

Building on this biological framework, the collected literature suggests that the matrix metalloproteinase pathway is a central driver of arthritis pathogenesis across rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, septic arthritis, spondyloarthritis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis because it couples inflammatory activation to irreversible joint tissue destruction. Broad reviews indicate that matrix metalloproteinases are consistently elevated in arthritic joints and, together with other proteases, degrade proteoglycans, collagens, and additional extracellular matrix constituents, thereby promoting cartilage loss and structural remodeling; in rheumatoid arthritis this proteolysis can also generate remnant epitopes that perpetuate autoimmunity, whereas in osteoarthritis collagenase thirteen produced by chondrocytes is a key effector of mechanically and inflammatory induced cartilage degeneration (PubMed:37161083, PubMed:37522140, PubMed:36647647). Mechanistically, synovial fibroblasts emerge as a major cellular source of pathogenic matrix metalloproteinases: disease-associated fibroblasts are polarized toward tissue-destructive states by transcriptional regulators such as ETS proto-oncogene one, which coordinates matrix metalloproteinase expression together with receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa B ligand, thereby promoting cartilage and bone damage even when inflammation is not proportionally changed (PubMed:35999392). Multiple upstream inflammatory circuits induce this pathway in arthritis, including interleukin one beta, tumor necrosis factor, interleukin seventeen A, granulocyte macrophage colony-stimulating factor, mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, nuclear factor kappa B signaling, Janus kinase two and signal transducer and activator of transcription three signaling, oxidative stress, and microRNA-mediated suppression of suppressor of cytokine signaling three; these signals converge on enhanced expression of matrix metalloproteinases such as matrix metalloproteinase one, matrix metalloproteinase three, matrix metalloproteinase nine, and matrix metalloproteinase thirteen in synovial fibroblasts and joint tissues, amplifying inflammation, pannus invasiveness, osteoclastogenesis, and matrix destruction (PubMed:32071294, PubMed:29394098, PubMed:26081345, PubMed:36427113, PubMed:17129374). Experimental arthritis studies further show that matrix metalloproteinase dysregulation is temporally linked to acute inflammatory phases and proteoglycan loss, while the balance with tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinoproteinases, especially tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases three, influences the extent of damage (PubMed:15642138, PubMed:37161083). Clinically, circulating or local levels of matrix metalloproteinases, particularly matrix metalloproteinase three and matrix metalloproteinase nine, correlate with disease activity, structural progression, and treatment response in rheumatoid arthritis and spondyloarthritis, and effective therapies such as rituximab or experimental interventions including nuclear receptor subfamily one group D member one agonism, kefir peptides, melatonin, curcumin-related strategies, and other matrix metalloproteinase-targeted approaches reduce matrix metalloproteinase expression in parallel with improvement in synovitis, cartilage preservation, and reduced bone erosion (PubMed:25190551, PubMed:35049445, PubMed:28420081, PubMed:32071294, PubMed:36682523, PubMed:38423225). Taken together, these publications support the view that the matrix metalloproteinase pathway is not merely a downstream marker of arthritis but rather a multifunctional pathogenic network that integrates inflammatory signaling, fibroblast and macrophage activation, extracellular matrix degradation, and bone remodeling, making it highly relevant for biomarker development, patient stratification, and targeted therapy.[PubMed:37161083](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37161083) [PubMed:32071294](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32071294) [PubMed:37522140](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37522140) [PubMed:17129374](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17129374) [PubMed:15642138](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15642138) [PubMed:38035026](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38035026) [PubMed:35999392](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35999392) [PubMed:35049445](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35049445) [PubMed:28420081](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28420081) [PubMed:25190551](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25190551) [PubMed:36682523](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36682523) [PubMed:36647647](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36647647) [PubMed:29394098](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29394098) [PubMed:36427113](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36427113) [PubMed:26081345](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26081345) [PubMed:38423225](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38423225) 

To connect this literature-based interpretation with the pathway-level enrichment result, the identified protein set may be viewed as a compact representation of the broader biological processes described above. There were 6 arthritis-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing matrix metalloproteinases as zinc-dependent endopeptidases that regulate extracellular matrix degradation, matrix remodeling, inflammatory signaling, immune cell behavior, angiogenesis, oxidative stress responses, cartilage erosion, and bone destruction. In quantitative terms, this enrichment set contains 6 proteins linked to a single highly disease-relevant biological process in arthritis, supporting a focused functional signal centered on dysregulated extracellular matrix turnover, synovial inflammation, and joint tissue damage, with particular relevance to cartilage, synovium, tendon, and bone biology.
